/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.headline: Jackdaw gasfield approved, boosting Shell and Equinor's North Sea operations
/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham's government will give the go-ahead to the Jackdaw gasfield on Wednesday, confirming its commitment to the North Sea fossil fuel industry; climate campaigners and some Labour MPs are expected to object.

Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey, the energy secretary and chancellor respectively, will make the announcement from Aberdeen on Wednesday morning after more than a year spent weighing whether doing so would violate the UK's climate commitments.

The approval for drilling at one of the biggest undeveloped fields in the declining North Sea basin gives a big boost to Britain's oil and gas industry – and especially to Shell and the Norwegian company Equinor, which operate it.

Climate campaigners will greet the decision with outrage, saying it undermines Labour's green credentials and will exacerbate the climate crisis.

Tessa Khan, the executive director of the anti-oil campaign group Uplift, said: “Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly 10 years. It has been oversold and won't stop the overall decline in North Sea jobs, as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely.”

She added: “Labour's climate credibility is on the line. No new oil and gasfields are compatible with safe climate limits.”

Once fully operational, Jackdaw will account for 6% of North Sea gas production, making it one of the biggest gasfields not yet in production.

Along with the Rosebank oilfield, its approval has become symbolic of the government's commitment to an oil and gas industry facing heavy job losses as reserves decline and platforms become increasingly automated.

The Conservative government approved the field in 2022, with ministers arguing it would help shield the UK from volatility in the energy market caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Labour came to power in 2024 promising not to grant new North Sea licences, not expecting to have to decide on Jackdaw or Rosebank.

A landmark ruling last year cast both fields into doubt, after a court found their environmental approval had been incorrectly granted.

The judge ruled that regulators should have taken into account the carbon emissions generated by burning the oil and gas the fields would produce when deciding whether they would violate the UK's climate commitments.

Shell and Equinor resubmitted their application for environmental consent last September, after which Fahnbulleh and her predecessor, Ed Miliband, spent months deciding whether to use their ministerial power to block it.

Both the prime minister and his predecessor, Keir Starmer, have come under heavy pressure to allow the fields to go ahead in recent months, not least from Donald Trump, who urged both men to “open up the North Sea”.

Burnham signalled this summer that he was sympathetic to the US president's arguments, promising to take a “pragmatic approach” to the decision.

“There is a resource there,” he said in July. “When people are struggling – you can't ignore that.”

He told the Commons last week: “I will take a pragmatic approach on oil and gas. We will set out our decisions shortly.”

Several sources have told the Guardian that Fahnbulleh has decided not to block the field, allowing the North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA), which regulates the industry, to give the go-ahead on financial and logistical grounds.

Making the announcement alongside Healey and the NSTA's chief executive, Stuart Payne, they will say the environmental approval does not breach Labour's manifesto commitment because it is not a new licence.

Fahnbulleh has not yet made a final decision on the larger Rosebank field, but energy department officials are already looking at ways the tax proceeds from the project could fund green projects if it goes ahead; a decision is expected later this year.

The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour's position in north-east Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have campaigned heavily for the permits to be granted.

It is likely to cause unease among some Labour MPs, however, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party.

A poll by Savanta for the climate group E3G, seen by the Guardian, found that nearly a third of voters say they would be less likely to vote Labour if it gives the go-ahead for more North Sea oil drilling.

That includes almost exactly a third of those who voted Labour at the last election, and around half of 18- to 24-year-olds.

Ellie Mae O'Hagan, the UK energy programme lead at E3G, said: “After a summer of deadly heatwaves, the public has made up its mind: more drilling is the wrong answer.

“If the prime minister wants a decade in power to change the country, he should invest in heat pumps and solar, not tax breaks for the oil and gas companies driving up our bills and polluting the planet.”

Officials say, however, that the Rosebank decision is likely to be the more sensitive one, partly because it would produce around seven times the CO2 emissions of Jackdaw and partly because most of the oil produced there would be exported.

Khan said: “The defining test is Rosebank. Burnham must deliver on his promise and prioritise affordable bills, genuine industrial growth and a safe climate over oil profits. That means rejecting Rosebank.”

/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.headline: New footage shows Reform official's doubts before £72m donations were made
/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.bodyHtml:
A senior Reform UK official raised questions about whether major donations from billionaire backers Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo would be legal under a proposed new foreign donors cap, three months before they gave £72m to the party.

James Orr was suspended as Reform's head of policy last month, after Channel 4 broadcast separate undercover footage in which he appeared to discuss ways to get around funding laws to allow donations from a US-based donor.

The matter is under police investigation and he remains suspended, although Reform has released its own report clearing Orr and another official of wrongdoing.

Orr, who was then Reform UK's head of policy and a Cambridge professor, had discussed potential difficulties around future donations from Harborne and Delo in undercover footage captured by the investigative reporting group Verbatim.

A reporter was posing as a potential donor when Orr talked to him about “filling the war chest in anticipation” of tougher donations rules, describing it as the establishment trying to “kneecap” the party.

The Guardian has now been shown the new footage after a public debate about whether the two £36m donations from Harborne and Delo to Reform UK will be allowed under the cap; the party maintains the donations are legal, pointing out that the retrospective overseas donor cap has not yet been passed into law.

In the footage, recorded in July this year, Orr expressed doubt about whether Delo and Harborne would still be able to donate given that, when it does become law, the £100,000 overseas donor cap is to cover party donations dating back to March this year.

Orr believed Delo would probably meet the residency test as long as he was not required to have been a tax resident, in which case he would be “stuffed”. He said Harborne was “probably more of a challenge” in terms of avoiding the overseas cap and he “can't do anything for 12 months” after moving back.

Harborne had been living in Thailand until he registered to vote in Hampshire this summer, and Delo has long been resident in Hong Kong, though he has been on the UK domestic register for some years.

The new law will limit overseas donors to giving £100,000 a year to a political party. It will apply to donations made after March 2026, and will require any domestic donor who wants to give more than £100,000 to have been resident in the UK for at least a year.

In the discussion, Orr was recorded as saying the party was too reliant on Harborne and Delo as “two big whales”. He said the new law was “a retrospective law, which is unheard of. So, we're going to challenge it in the courts.”

Orr added: “We'll push it through judicial review. And then … so, we'll have a big fight. But, yeah, the last few days we've been working hard on just filling the war chest as best we can, in anticipation of something quite brutal.”

On whether the two men would be caught by the overseas cap, he said: “I mean, there's going to be a huge fight over that. But Ben, I think it's probably OK, because I think he is … it depends on how they legislate it, they might just say, you must have been tax domiciled here for X period of time, in which case Ben is stuffed.”

Orr went on to say: “It depends what … test for moving back you apply. So, under the common law, there's a two-limb test, which is actually quite a – not a stringent one. It's a factual thing, a factual matrix test.

“How much time you spend in England, do you have a house here, can you vote, do you have any bills that you pay, you know, it's quite kind of, it's not tax … So, on that test, Ben meets it, I think. And then the second then is intention. Do you intend to stay, so, evidence that you intend to stay …”

Having debated whether Delo would meet the test, Orr said Harborne was “probably more of a challenge”. The Reform official said he would move back to the UK. “But, if he does move back, there's 12 – he can't pay – he can't do anything for 12 months. And, it looks as if they will bring that in.”

In his chat with the undercover reporter, Orr also referred to the “complicated backstory” of Delo, a British-born billionaire who was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls in his cryptocurrency business. He was later pardoned by Donald Trump.

Orr also spoke about having spent time on a boat with Ben Delo in the Peloponnese this summer, talking of mixing work and a holiday in Greece, saying: “We went from Athens down to Ben's boat in Porto Cheli.” Lawyers for Delo said he did not own a yacht.

A Reform UK spokesperson said: “We are 100% confident both [donations] are legal and won't ever have to be handed back.”

Orr did not respond to a request for comment. He has previously denied wrongdoing in relation to electoral laws on overseas funding and dismissed Verbatim as “politically motivated actors trying to discredit a political opponent through dubious legal means”.

Lawyers for Harborne described Orr's comments as private speculation that would not be appropriate to comment on and did not represent established facts. Delo's lawyers did not respond substantively, saying he would not be drawn into speculation about a conversation he was not party to, or the legal effect of a law yet to be passed. They later added that he had taken extensive legal advice on his donations and had previously set out his rationale for making them.

Reform has previously said it intends to take legal action against Verbatim and its directors over the undercover filming.

/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.headline: Ukraine again getting US warnings of Russian missile strikes, Zelenskyy says
/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.bodyHtml:
The US has resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv about Russian missile strikes, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday after a meeting with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway.

He said Ukraine was again receiving advance warnings of ballistic missile attacks, which had seemingly been suspended last week by the White House. “Now it works. It's great,” he said, adding that the US move would save lives.

The Ukrainian president said: “It's very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic [missiles] is coming. So we are thankful to the American side.”

Witkoff will on Wednesday meet Russian president Vladimir Putin after what a US official called “constructive” talks with Zelenskyy in Norway. The US envoy would aim to “create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations”, a US official told Reuters.

The talks in Oslo took place amid the worst crisis in US-Ukraine relations since Putin's full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. Donald Trump has bitterly accused Zelenskyy of failing to end the war and has said Ukraine needs a new leader.

On Tuesday Trump again suggested Zelenskyy was the main obstacle to an agreement. “We want Zelensky to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office,” he said.

Trump also said he had asked Putin to release Stephen Hubbard – an American taken prisoner by Russian forces in occupied Ukraine – in a further sign of his growing public alliance with Moscow.

The US president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined Witkoff and Zelenskyy by video for the talks. Norway's prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, also took part, alongside EU and British security officials.

Zelenskyy said he had held a “positive” phone call earlier with the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio. Asked if Ukraine was now losing the war, after recent hostile US actions, Zelenskyy replied: “Of course we are not losing. But we are losing people because of Russian attacks and time. It's a pity.”

He said he had raised with Rubio restrictions imposed last week on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk's satellite internet service. The slowdown has crippled Ukraine's ability to launch mid-range drone strikes on Russian battlefield positions.

Zelenskyy said he had offered to stop Ukraine's long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries – a key Trump demand – if the US provided Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors. The Pentagon has blocked the delivery of Patriots to Kyiv paid for by other countries, leaving Kyiv more vulnerable than ever to air attacks.

Speaking on Tuesday, Zelenskyy also said he opposed a trilateral summit floated by Putin, which would see the Russian leader, Trump and China's president, Xi Jinping, meet next month to strike a Ukraine deal. Zelenskyy would be shut out, the Wall Street Journal reported.

“There can be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in Oslo. He added: “If it's about Ukraine and our future it can only be acceptable when we are at the table of negotiations.”

The Washington-Kyiv crisis began 10 days ago when Trump announced he was lifting US sanctions on Russian diesel, in an attempt to lower fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. He then announced an energy ceasefire, which Kyiv implemented for several days but Russia ignored.

Despite this, Trump has bitterly rounded on Zelenskyy. He has effectively positioned the US as Russia's ally, favouring Moscow over Kyiv, to the dismay of America's pro-Ukrainian European and British backers. The US's peace proposals have largely echoed Russia's maximalist demands.

The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, on Tuesday questioned whether US negotiators had been honest brokers in the peace efforts. Witkoff has held numerous meetings with Putin in Moscow, while so far visiting Kyiv only once.

“Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now,” Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin's terms “because Europe has been supporting Ukraine”, Kallas said.

Tuesday's talks came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of US politicians that he believed “some political decision has been made to slow down … support for us”.

US officials have denied this but have failed to explain convincingly why satellite communication services were curtailed or intelligence sharing temporarily cut off.

Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio insisted nothing had changed. He said Patriot interceptors were in short supply and were needed in other parts of the world, as well as for the US's own defence. “There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” he insisted.

At least nine people were killed in Ukraine on Tuesday. They included passengers who were travelling on the Kyiv to Odesa highway. A Russian drone struck two vehicles, killing three people and injuring four. One of the victims was the driver of a shuttle bus, which was on its way from the capital to a military cemetery.

/uk-news/2026/oct/21/firefighters-growin.headline: Government to hold wildfire summit as MPs call for statutory water duty
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/firefighters-growin.bodyHtml:
Concerns have been raised about how drought affects the UK's ability to cope with wildfires, after MPs were told firefighters struggled for water supplies during this year's record summer.

MPs on the environment, food and rural affairs (EFRA) committee have called for water for firefighting to be recognised as a critical public safety requirement, saying the government should establish a statutory framework and national protocol setting out water companies' responsibilities during major fire incidents, including minimum expectations for water supply and pressure, communication and operational coordination with fire and rescue.

The committee also said water companies should be required to assess, test and verify their ability to support firefighting operations.

“Water companies must be relied upon for adequate supply,” the committee chair, Alistair Carmichael of the Scottish Liberal Democrats, said.

A government spokesperson said: “Improving wildfire preparedness is a major government priority. That's why this week we are holding a summit with government ministers, fire and rescue leaders, land managers and other partners to understand how we can strengthen the response to this increasing risk.”

A government-funded UK wildfire conference is scheduled to take place in Leeds on 10 and 11 November.

The government has also been urged to set out water companies' statutory responsibilities during major fire incidents more broadly, to improve the country's preparedness for the years ahead.

The UK experienced its hottest-ever summer this year, with prolonged dry periods and extreme heat fuelling wildfires across the country. Figures released earlier this month showed a clear upward trend in the number of fires recorded each year.

The chair of the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC), Phil Garrigan, told MPs on the EFRA committee that fires developed more quickly because of limited water supplies. He said concerns about water availability had grown during his 37 years in the fire service.

During a wildfire in Stourbridge in the West Midlands that destroyed several homes, replenishing a water carrier took almost 40 minutes because of reduced water pressure.

In tackling a separate wildfire in the New Forest in August, the fire service said maintaining water supply had been a significant challenge.

Fire services take water from mains and open sources such as lakes and rivers. With levels in the latter extremely low as a result of the drought, the fire service's access was restricted. It also faced pressure to limit its use of mains water to avoid shortages for paying customers.

“In summers like this year, we would normally ask for more resources, but those resources aren't always available and we're having to wait longer for additional resources or we're having to find other ways to deal with the fire,” said Dave Swallow, the NFCC's deputy lead on wildfires.

A survey of UK fire and rescue services in the summer found that 81% of respondents had changed their emergency response plans in areas where access to water was a concern.

The NFCC, which conducted the survey, said growing pressure from climate breakdown, population growth, housing development and emerging infrastructure such as datacentres, was increasing demand on an already stretched water network.

“Firefighters cannot fight fires without water. That sounds obvious, yet our evidence shows four in five fire and rescue services have had to change response plans because of concerns about firefighting water supplies,” Garrigan said in the summer.

As the climate crisis worsens and demand for water increases, the Environment Agency estimates that England's public water supply could be short by 5bn litres a day by 2055 without urgent action to future-proof resources.

/news/2026/oct/20/schools-in-england-mus.headline: Government expected to accept new antisemitism protections for schools
/news/2026/oct/20/schools-in-england-mus.bodyHtml:
The government is expected to accept the review's 27 recommendations, including provision of resources to tackle antisemitism in schools and dedicated teacher training in antisemitism awareness, including a national hotline where school leaders can quickly get advice on tackling antisemitism.

Other recommendations include encouraging schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance working definition of antisemitism, as well as strengthening teaching of the Holocaust to ensure that antisemitism is seen as a central theme of the genocide.

Policies on staff behaviour should also make clear that antisemitism is not acceptable, and that all schools and colleges should have “robust” reporting and response procedures.

The review's conclusions would require schools and colleges in England to recognise antisemitism as a distinct category of harm and take explicit action against it.

Sir David Bell, the former chief inspector of Ofsted who was commissioned by the government to lead the independent review, told Sky News that “a general commitment to tackling racism or prejudice or hate has not properly identified antisemitism as a particular kind of hate”, with the review, to be published on Wednesday, recommending increased awareness and teaching.

“We do need to name antisemitism as a particular kind of prejudice and hate, because I think if you don't name it, you don't actually know what you're tackling or what you're going to be able to do to respond to it,” Bell said.

“This is not just a report for Jewish children in Jewish schools. This is for all children and young people in all schools and colleges. We know that antisemitism crosses all boundaries,” Bell told the BBC.

Bell added there needs to be stronger guidance on political impartiality for schools so that students can “debate topical and difficult issues without feeling that teachers are imposing their own views on students”.

Bell's review found that three in five Jewish students said they had been affected by antisemitism, prompting schools and colleges in England to be expected to take a tougher stance.

Bell, who led the independent review, said he found many cases of antisemitism going unreported or unchallenged by students and teachers.

A survey conducted for the review found that one in five students said they had witnessed antisemitism, and three in five Jewish students had experienced it. However, fewer than half of those surveyed felt it would be addressed if reported.

The review was launched by the government in March, after antisemitic episodes including the attack at Manchester's Heaton Park synagogue in October last year.

The Community Security Trust (CST), which provides security and support to the Jewish community and schools, has published figures showing rising numbers of antisemitic incidents at schools this year.

In the first half of 2026 the CST found that reports of antisemitism in schools had reached the highest levels it had ever recorded, from 112 incidents in the first half of 2025 to 178 recorded over the same period in 2026.

A spokesperson from the Board of Deputies of British Jews said: “Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children's safety, and will strengthen accountability.”

Bell's review will be presented to MPs in parliament on Wednesday.

/australia-news/2026/oct/21/no-bail-bren.headline: Victoria to set up centralised process to monitor threats against MPs
/australia-news/2026/oct/21/no-bail-bren.bodyHtml:
The head of the Australian federal police has condemned a “febrile” political environment that has seen one person charged every week over the alleged threatening of MPs, as Victoria announces new steps to protect politicians.

But the AFP and Victoria police insist they had no intelligence to suggest 43-year-old Brendan Nugent would go on to allegedly drive a Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP Helen Haines in a targeted attack.

Haines has lost a leg and remains in a critical but stable condition in Melbourne's Alfred hospital. Doctors have been working to save her other leg.

Nugent appeared at the Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday morning on charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and a federal offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official, along with cannabis possession.

In court, Nugent looked downcast in a grey jumper and stared straight ahead. The Tarrawingee man did not request bail, and will remain in custody until a committal mention on 4 February.

Magistrate Allison Vaughan noted Nugent had mental health and neurological concerns, and that this was his first time in custody. She asked for a mental health professional to see Nugent immediately after his court appearence.

His lawyer, Chirag Patel, said his client was not on any prescribed medication and was not withdrawing from any substances. Patel said Nugent was also suffering from concussion and idiopathic transverse myelitis – a rare inflammatory disorder of the spinal cord.

Further charges considered

At an earlier press conference in Melbourne, Victoria police's chief commissioner, Mike Bush, said investigators were considering whether to lodge further charges against Nugent.

“That's always a consideration,” Bush said. “Of course, we have to locate and follow the evidence, but this is a very serious and tragic incident, and we will be looking at all serious charges.”

Bush also said: “There was nothing known to us that would have arisen, or piqued our interest, or given any indication that [Nugent] was an immediate threat.”

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

At the same press conference, the AFP commissioner, Krissy Barrett, was asked whether her team was aware of Nugent's social media posts, which included references to conspiracy theories and conflict in the Middle East.

“We didn't have any specific intelligence that would have indicated something as atrocious as happened on Monday afternoon,” Barrett said.

“I can confirm we had no holdings or no intelligence to suggest that there was any threat to MP Haines.”

Bush said Victoria police had deployed more staff to Wangaratta to assure the local community, but said he was confident this was an isolated incident.

'Growing volume of online abuse'

While Barrett and Bush did not allege a motive behind the alleged attack on Haines, which is still under investigation, they made general comments about the rising threat to MPs.

“The shocking alleged attack yesterday is what many had been dreading for some time,” Barrett said.

The AFP and Australia's domestic intelligence agency, Asio, will provide additional safety briefings to federal MPs on Wednesday. Around six of these sessions have been held this year.

Barrett said federal MPs were increasingly worried about threats, and referenced a “growing volume of online abuse, threatening rhetoric, and intimidation, increasing political polarisation and anti-government sentiment”.

She continued to raise concerns about “conspiracy-driven and grievance-based behaviours, lone actors motivated by a convergence of personal grievance, mental health vulnerabilities, and ideological concerns, and the potential for violence to emerge with little or no forewarning – particularly where individuals have no previous protection intelligence footprint”.

Bush highlighted similar concerns and said Victoria police would create a centralised process to help monitor threats against MPs.

“We want a single stop shop to report these things and have the ability to be very proactive,” Bush said.

On Tuesday, the Victorian Animal Justice party MP Georgie Purcell said she had received more security support as the partner of the federal MP, Josh Burns, than she did in her own role.

She urged Victoria police to create a dedicated unit, similar to that which exists within the AFP for politicians or people in high-profile roles.

“They have teams that can monitor fixated people, shifts in language, in behaviour, see if they're escalating, and then work out whether the continued behaviour could constitute an event,” Purcell says.

Bush, who will address state MPs and ministers on Wednesday afternoon, said there were no resourcing restraints that would prevent Victorian politicians from receiving the protection they felt they deserved.

/society/2026/oct/21/weight-loss-in-midd.headline: Losing just 5% of body weight in midlife can restore heart health, study finds
/society/2026/oct/21/weight-loss-in-midd.bodyHtml:
Losing just 5% of your body weight in middle age can reduce inflammation, lower the risk of stroke and make your heart as healthy as if you had never gained weight, research suggests.

Millions of men and women worldwide gain weight as they age, putting extra stress on their body, reducing quality of life and doing significant damage to their cardiovascular and metabolic health.

While most know being overweight or obese can affect health, many believe it is an inevitable part of ageing or assume they would need to shed a large amount of weight to reap any benefits.

The new study adds to growing evidence that small changes in body weight can have a big impact on health risks. While millions of people hope to lose a large amount of weight, it's much easier to start with a smaller goal and keep it off, experts said.

Researchers at University College London found overweight people who lost just 5% of their weight in their 40s and 50s had similar heart health in older age as adults who had always been a healthy weight.

By the time they reached the age of 62, both groups had comparable cholesterol levels, blood pressure and signs of inflammation – all key measures of cardiovascular and metabolic health.

The study's lead author, Charis Bridger-Staatz, of UCL's centre for longitudinal studies, said: “Ageing is often framed in terms of inevitable health decline, but our new research shows that this need not be the case.

“Just a modest reduction in weight in people's 50s may make a real difference to their health, potentially improving their quality of life and reducing their risk of heart issues.”

Having poor metabolic or cardiovascular health can raise the risk of serious conditions, including type 2 diabetes, heart disease and cardiovascular events such as heart attacks or strokes.

Bridger-Staatz, a senior research fellow in population health, said thousands of lives could be lost needlessly in the next decade because of poor health related to being overweight or obese.

“While obesity prevention strategies rightly place strong emphasis on children and young people, these findings indicate that prevention efforts should also extend to people in their 50s,” she added.

“Although this is often perceived as a stage of life when meaningful health change is no longer possible, our research shows that it's never too late to start making changes to improve your health.”

In the study, researchers looked at data from more than 6,000 people born in the UK in 1958. They analysed body mass index and noted the highest BMI each person reached by the age of 42.

The team then examined whether people had lost or gained at least 5% of their weight by age 50, and if they had maintained this weight difference at age 55. Measurements such as blood pressure, cholesterol and inflammation markers were also analysed.

The study found that at the age of 62, the metabolic and cardiovascular health of overweight people who had lost weight in middle age closely resembled that of the consistently healthy weight group.

This was an observational study, so conclusions cannot be drawn about cause and effect. The researchers also highlighted other limitations but said the findings had important implications.

The study's co-author, Laura Gimeno, said: “These results show that the benefits of weight loss may extend beyond short-term weight reduction. Our findings support current interest around expanding access to effective weight-loss support, including weight-loss medications.

“They also highlight the importance of reducing further weight gain in midlife, as this was consistently linked to the fastest deterioration in heart and metabolic health.”

/world/2026/oct/21/hastings-british-muse.headline: Hastings schoolchildren secure visit to see the Bayeux tapestry
/world/2026/oct/21/hastings-british-muse.bodyHtml:
The MP for Hastings and Rye, Helena Dollimore, has secured access to the Bayeux tapestry for schoolchildren across Hastings after lobbying the British Museum. “To be fair to the museum, that has been a success,” she said.

A British Museum spokesperson said: “Demand for the Bayeux tapestry exhibition has been exceptionally high. In recognition of the area's historic connection to the Battle of Hastings we agreed to offer residents the chance to secure tickets before their wider release.

“All residents are still able to book tickets as part of the general sale on 21 October and will have further opportunities in the new year when the third tranche of tickets are released.”

“This offer is not guaranteed access – it is on a first-come, first-served basis in the same way tickets for the exhibition are on sale to our members and the public.”

Hastings residents have missed out on tickets for the Bayeux tapestry after being put on hold for hours by a “glitchy and shambolic” phone system, their MP has said.

People from “1066 Country” were promised a chance to buy before a sales line opened to the public on Wednesday. But Dollimore said it has been almost impossible for her constituents to get through to the British Museum.

Hastings residents were told they could get early access to book the latest release of tickets from Monday this week by calling the British Museum box office and providing proof of their address. But Dollimore said her constituents were left on hold for hours.

“Why do my constituents have to work on a glitchy phone line when online booking is clearly possible for others?” she asked.

“One person booked after two hours and 38 minutes in the queue, another said he was on hold for two and a half hours.

“If you can't get access right for the people in the place this tapestry tells the story of, you need to sort that out before you start letting people jump the queue.”

VIP guests including Maya Jama, Mick Jagger and senior staff at Samsung and Bloomberg have had no such issues gaining access to Bayeux viewings, having attended star-studded balls and dinners held in the tapestry room since September.

Celebrities, businesspeople and politicians flocked to the museum on Saturday for a ball. The guest of honour, tech billionaire Igor Tulchinsky, posed next to the host, Rosanna Konarzewski, a communications executive who was wearing a sweeping ballgown made of a replica Bayeux tapestry. Sources in attendance said that while the general public have been banned from taking pictures of the embroidery, some ball guests managed to photograph it.

The Guardian revealed that another tech billionaire, Peter Thiel, was given a VIP tour of the embroidery before it opened to the public. Guests of the One Aldwych hotel are also allowed to view the tapestry if they book a £1,000-a-night room.

Dollimore said: “I had a constituent who waited for hours with her elderly parent who was in her 80s, and they were sent away because of a corporate event. They promised the people of 1066 Country would be able to get access to the tapestry, but seem to be prioritising these corporates.”

The MP has unsuccessfully tried to get tickets for herself and her family. “I have been trying since 10am to get through, and even I can't,” she said.

Members of the public faced online queues of up to nine hours when tickets went on sale for the first time this summer. There were reports of 40,000 people queueing by mid-morning, with that figure ballooning to almost 80,000 by mid-afternoon.

The 70-metre (229ft) tapestry, which is made of linen with embroidered images of events surrounding the Battle of Hastings in 1066, arrived in the UK in July for the first time in nearly 1,000 years.

Adult tickets cost £33 in peak hours and £27 at other times, compared with the €12 (£10) fee at the artwork's home in Bayeux, Normandy.
